verdicts.lens: Identity & ABDM: Keycloak org/sub mapping, a doctor at two hospitals, token replay across subdomains, ABDM callback routing to the right tenant, HPR/HFR ids

serious_gaps.gap: Cloning from tpl_base copies external_id UUIDs into every tenant. This breaks the design's claim that 'CARE JWTs are tenant-bound because external_id is random per schema', and it creates a cross-tenant leak through the ABHA/UHID identifier-config cache.
serious_gaps.evidence: Design: 'CARE's own JWTs are naturally bound to one tenant, because users are looked up by an external_id that is random per schema' and 'clone_schema from tpl_base ... the clone keeps integer ids'. SIMPLE_JWT USER_ID_FIELD='external_id' (config/settings/base.py:411). clone_schema copies rows verbatim, so every seeded row (identifier configs for UHID, ABHA number and ABHA address, questionnaires, value sets, and any User created while seeding) has the same external_id in every tenant. PatientIdentifierConfigCache.configs is a process-wide class dict keyed by config external_id (care/emr/models/patient.py:186-198), read at care/emr/resources/patient/spec.py:278 and :288. Clearing it only affects the current process. The design explicitly leaves this dict alone ('keyed by UUID external_id, so it is left as is'). So once hospital A edits or retires its seeded ABHA config, hospital B is served A's serialised config from the same worker. Any User row in tpl_base would also exist with the same external_id and password hash everywhere, so a CARE JWT for that user replays across all hospitals. The canary crawl ('GET by each of A's ids ... expect 404') will also hit B's identical seeded ids.
serious_gaps.fix: After clone_schema, re-key data (UPDATE ... SET external_id=gen_random_uuid() for every BaseModel table) as part of ihr_create_tenant, or seed packs per tenant instead of cloning data rows. Add a CI assertion that tpl_base contains zero rows in users_user, authtoken_token, django_session and ihr_identity_staffidentity. Also add the schema to PatientIdentifierConfigCache.configs keys (one more line in the existing signals/patient patch), or add a schema-scoped wrapper. Change the canary test to crawl only ids created after cloning.

serious_gaps.gap: The ABDM correlation row is written inside the request's atomic transaction, so on-* callbacks race the commit and get rejected (or rows are lost when the request rolls back).
serious_gaps.evidence: Design: 'Every outbound call from a tenant writes (request_id, hospital, kind, expires_at) in the same transaction, before it sends', and on-* callbacks are 'looked up in public AbdmCorrelation'; 'If ... nothing resolves, reject (4xx)'. ATOMIC_REQUESTS=True (config/settings/base.py:73) keeps the whole request in one uncommitted transaction. The callback arrives on a separate connection and transaction and cannot see the row until the initiating request commits. ABDM gateway callbacks are asynchronous and can arrive within milliseconds. If the request later fails and rolls back after the HTTP send, the correlation disappears even though the gateway acted on the request.
serious_gaps.fix: Write AbdmCorrelation with an autocommit connection (a second DB alias for public writes) before sending. Alternatively, never call the gateway inside a request: enqueue the send with transaction.on_commit to a Celery task that writes the correlation and commits, then sends. Have the inbound bridge retry the lookup briefly (or park unmatched callbacks for N seconds) before rejecting. Add an isolation test where the callback is delivered before the originating request commits.

serious_gaps.gap: HFR id ownership and routing trust are under-specified. Routing does not require a verified route, the verification flow is undefined, and the unique hfr_id constraint conflicts with a facility that is both HIP and HIU.
serious_gaps.evidence: Design: HfrFacilityRoute has 'hfr_id: unique; ... role: HIP or HIU; active; verified_at', 'verified_at is set only after the HFR verification flow', yet inbound resolution simply says 'look it up in public HfrFacilityRoute'. The row is mirrored from a tenant-side ABDM profile that hospital admins edit, so first-come squatting is possible. A tenant that enters another hospital's HFR id first claims the unique slot. If routing ignores verified_at, gateway discover, consent-notify and health-information requests carrying that X-HIP-ID (patient demographics, ABHA addresses) land in the squatter's schema. Separately, a hospital usually registers the same HFR id as both HIP and HIU; 'hfr_id unique' plus a single 'role' column rejects the second row. The design also never defines what 'HFR verification' proves.
serious_gaps.fix: Route only rows with active=True AND verified_at IS NOT NULL; unverified HFR ids are rejected and logged. Define verification as an ABDM-side fact: platform automation adds the service to our bridge, and verified_at is set only once GET /api/hiecm/gateway/v3/bridge-services shows it and the HFR facility manager has approved the link. Hospital admins must never be able to write HfrFacilityRoute; only a platform command, after an ops or HFR check. Change the constraint to unique(hfr_id, role), or make role a set, with a check that both roles of one hfr_id map to the same hospital.

serious_gaps.gap: HPR ids (Health Professional Registry) are not designed at all. Each hospital can attach any HPR id to any of its User rows, which allows practitioner impersonation in ABDM-shared FHIR bundles and e-prescriptions.
serious_gaps.evidence: The design names Keycloak sub, StaffIdentity and per-tenant User rows but never mentions HPR. docs/PLAN.md:277 only plans getting 'HPR for test doctors'. With one User row per hospital, an HPR id would naturally end up as a per-tenant field (a CARE user field or an ihr_abdm profile) that the hospital admin edits, and the design's own risk list says 'registration numbers or qualifications edited in one hospital do not propagate'. A doctor at two hospitals could have different or unverified HPR ids, and a hospital could stamp a real doctor's HPR id on documents written by someone else.
serious_gaps.fix: Treat the HPR id as a global, verified identity attribute. Store it on the Keycloak user (read-only to the user and to hospital admins), set it only through an HPR verification flow run by a platform service, and emit it as a token claim. The tenant User row mirrors it read-only through KeycloakAuthentication's claim sync, like the name. Practitioner identifiers in outbound ABDM bundles must come from that claim or mirror, never from tenant-editable fields. Add HPR-based de-duplication of Keycloak accounts (one HPR id maps to at most one sub).

serious_gaps.gap: The invite flow can enlist or take over other hospitals' staff. It matches on identifiers Keycloak cannot verify, adds membership without the invitee's acceptance, and reveals whether an account exists.
serious_gaps.evidence: Design: invite step 1 'finds or creates the Keycloak user by verified email or phone', and step 2 'adds the user as an unmanaged member of the hospital's org' before any acceptance. Keycloak 26 has no built-in phone verification, so a phone attribute is whatever the user or an admin typed. If it is user-editable in the user profile, an attacker who sets a victim doctor's phone is 'found' and added to the hospital instead. Admin-API email search returns users whether or not they are verified, unless emailVerified is checked. Because membership is created without consent, hospital A's admin can add Dr B (who works only at hospital B) to A. Dr B then appears in A's public booking list: FacilitySchedulableUsersViewSet has authentication_classes=[] and lists SchedulableResource users (care/emr/api/viewsets/facility.py:185-196). The 'found' vs 'created' outcome also lets one hospital probe whether a person is registered on the platform. Per-org identity providers, which the Keycloak Organizations feature supports, are not addressed. If a hospital's own IdP is linked with trust-email auto-linking, it can assert another hospital's doctor's email and take over their global account.
serious_gaps.fix: Match only on emailVerified=true email. Never match on phone, or make phone a read-only attribute that only an SMS-verification extension can set. Use Keycloak's org invitation (the user must accept) and create StaffIdentity and the active directory entry only after acceptance; until then the User row stays is_active=False and is not schedulable. Return the same response whether or not the account already existed. In the ADR, forbid per-org IdPs, or require them with no auto-link by email (link only through an authenticated first-broker-login re-auth). Disable self-registration in the realm.

serious_gaps.gap: Credential blast radius: the tenant-serving backend holds a realm-wide Keycloak admin credential, in the same realm as platform operators.
serious_gaps.evidence: Design: the invite endpoint (called by any hospital admin) uses 'the admin API with a service account limited to manage-users and manage-organizations'. Platform operators live in the same realm `indiehr` and are told apart only by a 'platform-operator' realm role. manage-users is realm-wide, so it can reset credentials and required actions for every user, operators included. Any RCE or SSRF in the CARE process (the largest attack surface, with hundreds of tenants' admins hitting it) therefore escalates to taking over operator accounts and every hospital's staff.
serious_gaps.fix: Move Keycloak admin calls into a separate provisioning worker (its own deployment and secret) that tenant web pods reach only through a narrow queue or API with per-tenant authorisation (the invite is for org X, and the caller is an admin of the tenant bound to X). Restrict the service account with Keycloak fine-grained admin permissions v2 to members of hospital orgs only. Put platform operators in a separate realm (or exclude them from FGAP scope), with their own console client, so that no tenant-side credential can touch them.

serious_gaps.gap: KeycloakAuthentication's checks are too loose for a realm that every tenant and client shares: no azp or typ check, multi-org tokens accepted everywhere, and no step-up or MFA (acr) binding across silent cross-hospital SSO.
serious_gaps.evidence: Design step 6 checks 'signature ... iss, aud, exp and nbf' and that 'some organization entry's id equals request.tenant.keycloak_org_id'. azp=indiehr-web is described as a token property but never validated, and typ is not checked. Any other realm client whose access tokens carry aud indiehr-api (console, future patient or analyzer clients, service accounts) is accepted wherever the sub has a StaffIdentity. A token requested with `organization:*` (any member can request it from the public SPA client) is valid at every hospital the user belongs to, so one XSS or leaked token on one hospital's origin works on all of them. This undoes the 'tokens stored per origin' isolation the design relies on. Silent `prompt=none` SSO means a session created at a hospital without MFA signs the user into a hospital that requires MFA, and the design never checks acr/amr.
serious_gaps.fix: Also require typ=='Bearer', azp in an explicit allow-list, and exactly one organization entry equal to request.tenant (reject multi-org tokens on tenant hosts; the SPA always asks for organization:<alias>). Require realm-wide MFA for staff, or check acr/amr per tenant policy and trigger step-up (prompt=login with acr_values) when it is not met. Add tests: an organization:* token, a token with a foreign azp, and an ID-token or refresh-token replay must all return 401/403.

serious_gaps.gap: Offboarding and revocation are unspecified. A removed doctor or a timed-out break-glass support user keeps access through valid access tokens and an active tenant User row until the nightly reconciler runs.
serious_gaps.evidence: Design: 'Keycloak is the source of truth, every request checks the org claim, and a nightly reconciler fixes the directory'. The org claim is only as fresh as the token. KeycloakAuthentication requires StaffIdentity→User.is_active, but removing someone from a Keycloak org does not touch the tenant row, and nothing synchronous deactivates it. Break-glass is 'time-boxed org membership', but Keycloak org membership has no expiry, so the design names no enforcer. CARE's own logout revocation (cache-keyed raw-token invalidation in config/authentication.py:18-22) does not apply to Keycloak tokens, and RP-initiated logout leaves other origins' access tokens valid until exp. Access-token lifespan is never pinned.
serious_gaps.fix: Pin the access-token lifespan to 5 minutes or less in the realm export and ADR. Have the removal flow, whether an admin action or a Keycloak admin-event listener, deactivate the tenant User and the directory entry synchronously. Check a revocation denylist keyed by sub+org (or the session id against back-channel logout events) in KeycloakAuthentication. Give break-glass an expires_at in TenantOperation, enforced per request and by a Celery job that removes the org membership and deactivates the row.

serious_gaps.gap: There is no working machine or service identity in production. The design removes TokenAuthentication and blocks POST /api/v1/users/, but CARE service accounts are created through that endpoint and authenticate only with authtoken; 'CustomJWTAuthentication for service tokens' has no issuer.
serious_gaps.evidence: The design says authtoken keys for the analyzer bridge 'are therefore valid in one hospital only', yet the production DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES is ('ihr_identity.authentication.KeycloakAuthentication', 'config.authentication.CustomJWTAuthentication'), which drops rest_framework.authentication.TokenAuthentication (config/settings/base.py:374). CARE mints service-account credentials as authtoken Token rows (care/emr/api/viewsets/user.py:233-262, Token.objects.create at :254). Service accounts are created with POST /api/v1/users/ and is_service_account=True (user.py:150-157), which TenantGuardMiddleware blocks. Local login (/api/v1/auth/login/, config/urls.py:35) is blocked too, so nothing ever mints the CARE JWTs the design keeps 'for service tokens'. A Keycloak client-credentials token has no StaffIdentity and so gets 403 'not provisioned'.
serious_gaps.fix: Choose one machine-identity path and write it in the ADR. Either keep TokenAuthentication in production, limited to is_service_account users (tenant-local by schema), with keys created only by a platform command, or use Keycloak client-credentials clients per tenant, bound to the org id through a client attribute and mapped to a tenant ServiceIdentity. Remove CustomJWTAuthentication from production if no issuer exists. Make the auth-endpoint block list come from the URL resolver; it currently misses /api/v1/otp/password_reset/, /api/v1/password_change/ and /api/v1/auth/token/refresh|verify/ (config/urls.py:37-63, config/api_router.py:126-127).

verdicts.summary:
The core identity model holds up through this lens: one global Keycloak sub, one org per hospital, and per-tenant User rows linked by StaffIdentity. Keeping User.external_id random per schema, binding on org UUID rather than alias, and adding the tenant-claim patch to PatientToken correctly close the obvious cross-subdomain replays. That includes the patient OTP path, which config/patient_otp_authentication.py:99-154 and care/emr/api/otp_viewsets/login.py:162-165 show is otherwise unbound. Nothing found is fatal, but several premises break against real behaviour:
- Cloning from tpl_base copies external_ids into every tenant. That undoes the 'random per schema' token binding, and the design deliberately keeps the UUID-keyed PatientIdentifierConfigCache (patient.py:186-198), which then leaks ABHA/UHID configs across tenants.
- With ATOMIC_REQUESTS=True (base.py:73), ABDM on-* callbacks race the uncommitted AbdmCorrelation row.
- HFR routing does not require verified routes, the verification flow is undefined, and the unique hfr_id constraint blocks a facility that is both HIP and HIU.
- HPR ids are missing from the design entirely.
- The invite flow matches on phone numbers Keycloak cannot verify and adds members without their acceptance.
- A realm-wide manage-users credential sits in the tenant-serving process, in the same realm as platform operators.
- Token validation does not check azp or typ, accepts multi-org tokens, and has no MFA/acr binding across silent SSO.
- Revocation and offboarding timing is unspecified.
- Service accounts cannot work in production as configured: TokenAuthentication is removed and user-create is blocked, yet the design relies on authtoken keys for the analyzer bridge.
Each gap has a contained fix. Review was read-only; key code is in /home/ubuntu/AI Projects/IndieHR/apps/backend/config/authentication.py, config/patient_otp_authentication.py, config/settings/base.py, care/emr/api/viewsets/user.py, care/emr/models/patient.py and care/emr/api/viewsets/facility.py.

verdicts.lens: Upstream sync and team burden: how many files we patch, conflict risk on monthly CARE syncs, the tests we must add, and whether a simpler alternative gives the same safety.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Cloning every tenant from tpl_base gives all tenants the same external_id UUIDs. That breaks the design's reason for leaving PatientIdentifierConfigCache unpatched, and it creates a cross-tenant leak through an in-process cache that is never invalidated.
fatal_flaws.evidence: The design says 'PatientIdentifierConfigCache.configs is keyed by UUID external_id, so it is left as is', and also says 'the clone keeps integer ids'. clone_schema copies rows, so it copies BaseModel.external_id as well (care/utils/models/base.py:16). The cache is a process-wide class dict keyed by config external_id (care/emr/models/patient.py:186-198). PatientIdentifierConfigCache.clear_cache is never called outside tests: the only callers of get_config are care/emr/resources/patient/spec.py:278,288. Every seeded PatientIdentifierConfig (UHID, ABHA number, ABHA address from pack core-in) therefore has the same UUID in every tenant. Once a gunicorn worker has served hospital A, it returns A's serialized config (display, regex, retrieve_config, including A's local edits) inside hospital B's patient responses, for the life of the process. The same shared UUIDs also make the canary crawl assertion 'no response contains any of A's external_ids' fail on every template-origin row (roles, value sets, questionnaires, configs). Engineers will then add exclusions, and those exclusions weaken the suite.
fatal_flaws.fix: Choose one of two options. (a) After clone_schema, regenerate external_id for every BaseModel table in the new schema in the same transaction (UPDATE ... SET external_id = gen_random_uuid()); this is safe because the template holds no patients or other UUID soft references. Add a test that no external_id is shared between two freshly provisioned tenants. (b) Stop cloning data and seed packs per tenant through Specs. Either way, also give PatientIdentifierConfigCache a schema-aware key (one more small logged patch next to the CACHED_CONFIG patch), because it has no invalidation even within a single tenant. Count this file in the patch budget.

serious_gaps.gap: The headline '6 small patches, about 40 lines' understates the real patch ledger. The six core patches are low-risk, but the files that actually cause sync conflicts are the ones left out of the count.
serious_gaps.evidence:
Upstream churn over the last 12 months (git log on upstream-backend/develop): config/celery_app.py 1 commit, patient_otp_token.py 0, signals/patient/base.py 1, models/valueset.py 0, utils/file_manager.py 0, file_uploads/cover_image.py 0. Conflict risk on the core six is therefore near zero. The grafts add more files:
- Pipfile and Pipfile.lock: 16 commits in 12 months. docs/UPSTREAM.md step 2 already says they 'conflict on most syncs'.
- care/emr/tasks/__init__.py (conditional).
- A 'tid' claim in CARE-issued staff tokens (config/auth_views.py or a token class).
- A FILE_OBJECT_KEY_PREFIX_FUNCTION hook, which is a different patch shape from the inline file_manager patch.
- PatientIdentifierConfigCache (see the fatal flaw above).
- Optionally AuthUserProvider.tsx.
- P1-T4's Login.tsx: 705 lines and 12 upstream commits in 12 months, the busiest file in the plan.
The real budget is about 11-13 files, and two of them conflict regularly.
serious_gaps.fix: Publish the full ledger in the ADR: file, lines, 12-month upstream churn and expected conflict rate for each. Keep the near-zero-churn core patches as designed. Treat Pipfile/lock and Login.tsx as the real recurring cost and work to shrink them (see the OIDC gap below). Tenancy libraries could go in a plugin requirements layer installed in our own Dockerfile stage, rather than in upstream's Pipfile, if the P0-T9 lock policy allows it.

serious_gaps.gap: The grafted design contradicts itself on storage keys and on the migration and downtime model, so the team cannot implement it as written. CARE's migrations are not expand/contract either.
serious_gaps.evidence:
Object keys: the file_manager and cover_image patches use 'tenants/<schema_name>/', while a graft says to use 't/<Hospital.uuid>/' through a settings hook. ADR-002 says 'tenants/<tenant_id>/'.
Migrations: the design says 'tenants not yet migrated keep serving on the old code, which is why changes must be expand/contract'. Grafts say to 503 any tenant whose schema_version does not match, and to use a platform-wide maintenance window for the pilot. Upstream ships contract steps in the same release as the code change, for example care/emr/migrations/0082_remove_encounter_encounter_class_history.py. Data migrations such as 0083 (merging duplicate InventoryItems) run once per tenant. Upstream added 61 migration files in 12 months and 9 in the last 6. With 'first failure stops the run', a mid-run failure leaves some tenants on old code and some on new, with no stated way to run two images at once. The pg_trgm graft also appears three times.
serious_gaps.fix:
Make one decision per topic before P1-T1:
- Prefix: one scheme. Hospital.uuid is better, because restores and renames are then harmless.
- v1 deployment: a single platform-wide maintenance window (around 02:00 IST). Set a budget of (per-schema migration time × N) / parallel, and use the staging preflight to enforce it.
- Remove the expand/contract wording until per-tenant cohorts with two live images are designed.
- Remove the duplicate grafts.
Record the result as an ADR-002 amendment.

serious_gaps.gap: Every isolation and parity check is scheduled for every push. That multiplies Apps CI time several times over for a one-developer team, on a dev machine that cannot run any of it locally.
serious_gaps.fix:
Split the checks into three tiers:
- Every push: structural FK and public-table checks, cache/lock/search_path unit tests, token-binding tests, and the URL-resolver lint.
- Nightly and every upstream sync: the tenant-mode CARE suite, the canary crawl, Celery, storage and mutation runs.
- Release only: restore drills, Playwright and migration timing at 50/200 schemas.
State the CI-minute budget in the ADR.

serious_gaps.gap: Blocking CARE auth endpoints by deny-list, and requiring a crawl fixture for every route, is costly on each sync and fails open. New upstream auth paths would arrive unblocked, or would stall the sync.
serious_gaps.evidence: config/urls.py:35-65 has eight auth and password routes. Twelve views set their own authentication_classes, so the overlay's DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES never applies to them. Examples: care/emr/api/otp_viewsets/login.py:123, care/users/api/otp_viewset/reset_password.py:52, care/emr/api/viewsets/mfa_login.py:29, care/users/reset_password_views.py:35,87,147, care/emr/api/viewsets/facility.py:190,223 and organization.py:62. Upstream added auth surface in the last year: OTP password reset (#3630, 2026-06) and service-account token endpoints (#3440, 2026-01). config/api_router.py has 85 registrations, and care/emr/api/viewsets saw 211 upstream commits in 12 months. The graft 'crawl fails when a new upstream route has no fixture' turns every route-adding sync into hand-written fixture work.
serious_gaps.fix: In production, have TenantGuardMiddleware fail closed. Keep an allow-list of reviewed (route, method, authentication_classes) tuples, and return 404 for any route not on it until a reviewer adds it. Generate the crawl from the URL resolver, with ids from model_bakery-created rows, so that a new route only needs a fixture when generation fails. The sync checklist then becomes 'review the new allow-list diffs' rather than 'notice the new endpoint'.

serious_gaps.gap: Settings-overlay drift. Several overlay choices fail silently when upstream changes settings, and there are cases where tests run in non-tenant mode while CI stays green.
serious_gaps.evidence:
- INSTALLED_APPS is rebuilt from SHARED_APPS and TENANT_APPS. If TENANT_APPS is a hand-maintained list, a new upstream app added to DJANGO/THIRD_PARTY/LOCAL_APPS (config/settings/base.py:110-141; base.py changed in 10 upstream commits over 12 months) is dropped.
- `MIDDLEWARE.insert(1, ...)` depends on position, and base.py:213-214 already inserts at index 0 when a flag is set.
- config/settings/test.py:43-55 redefines CACHES with no KEY_FUNCTION, so an overlay that only patches base-derived CACHES leaves the tenant-mode test run without tenant cache keys.
- Upstream's compose env sets DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=config.settings.deployment (apps/backend/docker/.prebuilt.env:9), and manage.py:16 uses setdefault. `make test` therefore runs CARE settings, not ihr_tenancy.conf.test, unless our compose override changes that.
serious_gaps.fix:
- Derive TENANT_APPS as [a for a in INSTALLED_APPS if a not in SHARED_APPS] from the upstream list.
- Insert the tenant middleware relative to 'django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware' by name, and assert the position.
- Apply the cache key function and engine through one helper that every env overlay calls.
- Add a Django system check, run in CI and at startup, that fails unless ENGINE is the django_tenants backend, every Redis cache has the tenant KEY_FUNCTION, both tenant middlewares are in the right order, and DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE starts with ihr_tenancy.conf.
- Set the module in deploy/ compose overrides rather than in upstream env files.

serious_gaps.gap: The '2,005 tests inside a tenant' gate does not plan for CARE's thread-based concurrency tests or its migration test. These will fail for runner reasons and could tempt edits to CARE tests.
serious_gaps.evidence: care/emr/tests/test_dispense_order_concurrency.py:1,73-77,121 (and test_delivery_order_concurrency.py, test_inventory_item_lock.py, test_inventory_lock_flows.py) start ThreadPoolExecutor workers and close and reopen connections. A new per-thread django-tenants connection starts in 'public', where no emr tables exist. care/emr/tests/test_inventory_item_migration.py:14-31 runs MigrationExecutor backwards and forwards on the live connection inside a TransactionTestCase.
serious_gaps.fix: In TenantDiscoverRunner, connect a connection_created receiver (test settings only) that calls set_schema('h_test') on every new connection. Explicitly cover TransactionTestCase flush and the MigrationExecutor test in the P1-T1 gate. Record 'fix the runner, never CARE tests' as a rule in docs/UPSTREAM.md.

serious_gaps.gap: The reference-pack pipeline is tightly coupled to CARE's Spec and model churn, and per-row content hashes will flag upstream schema changes as hospital edits. Pack validity is not tested on syncs.
serious_gaps.evidence: ihr_apply_refdata creates rows 'through CARE's own Spec or serializers' and stores 'per-row content hashes'. Over 12 months the Specs and models packs depend on changed often: questionnaire resources 7 commits, tag 7, observation_definition 4, charge_item_definition 4, models/questionnaire.py 7, models/charge_item_definition.py 4. If a migration adds or changes a defaulted field, the stored row hash no longer matches, and every seeded row in every tenant is reported as a conflict.
serious_gaps.fix: Hash only the fields the pack supplies, normalised through the Spec, not the stored row. Tag each pack with the CARE pin it was validated against. Add a sync-time CI job that applies every pack into a fresh tenant and re-applies it idempotently, with zero conflicts expected.

serious_gaps.gap: The planned Keycloak login patches Login.tsx, the busiest frontend file, and the design does not address the SPA's token-refresh loop. A smaller, lower-conflict alternative exists.
serious_gaps.evidence: apps/frontend/src/Providers/AuthUserProvider.tsx:68-92 polls authApi.tokenRefresh (/api/v1/auth/token/refresh/, src/types/auth/authApi.ts:37) in the background and deletes both tokens when the call fails. signOut calls /api/v1/auth/logout/ with {access, refresh} (lines 148-157). Request auth simply reads localStorage care_access_token (src/Utils/request/utils.ts:77-82). If CARE's auth endpoints are blocked, or are handed Keycloak tokens, users are logged out every refresh interval. Login.tsx has 705 lines and had 12 upstream commits in 12 months.
serious_gaps.fix: Use an ihr_identity backend shim at the same paths (token/refresh and logout proxied to Keycloak, enforced at the ingress), plus a same-origin /auth/callback page that completes PKCE and writes care_access_token and care_refresh_token. Then the only frontend patch is a small redirect in Login.tsx, or none if the ingress sends /login to the shim. Record this choice in the P1-T4 plan now, because it decides what TenantGuardMiddleware blocks.

serious_gaps.gap: The design rejects ADR-002's mandated second prototype without evidence, and its rejected-alternatives list omits the zero-patch baseline. The owner therefore cannot see the real cost of the trade.
serious_gaps.evidence: docs/adr/002-tenancy-schema-per-hospital.md:28-31 says 'P1-T1 must test both' django-tenants and a thin search_path middleware. The design rejects the middleware with an unsupported 'about 30%' figure and amends ADR-002 only on reference masters. Because every CARE app now sits in the tenant schema, django-tenants' shared/tenant app split goes almost unused. Its remaining value is clone_schema, the migrate_schemas executors and tenant-schemas-celery. Instance-per-tenant (a separate process set per hospital) needs no tenancy patches at all, but costs roughly 0.6-1 GB RAM per tenant, which is impractical at hundreds of tenants. That figure belongs in the ADR.
serious_gaps.fix: Keep django-tenants, which is still the cheaper path once Celery and cloning are counted, but either run the time-boxed comparison in P1-T1 or explicitly amend ADR-002's prototype clause. Add instance-per-tenant to the rejected alternatives, with its RAM and ops numbers, as the 'no upstream patches' baseline.

verdicts.summary:
Through this lens the core choice holds up well. Putting every CARE app in the tenant schema and keeping only our tables in public avoids FK and user-model patches. Its six core upstream patches touch files with almost no upstream churn (0-1 commits in 12 months each), so they will rarely conflict on monthly syncs. I found no schema-qualified raw SQL in CARE, and the patched S3 and raw-Redis sites are the only ones in the codebase. The burden is elsewhere.
1. Fatal: cloning tpl_base copies external_id UUIDs into every tenant. That breaks the stated reason for leaving PatientIdentifierConfigCache unpatched; it is a process-wide dict that is never invalidated (patient.py:186-198), so one hospital's identifier config reaches another. Fix it by regenerating UUIDs after the clone and keying that cache by schema.
2. The real patch ledger is about 11-13 files, not 6. Pipfile/lock (conflicts on most syncs) and Login.tsx (12 upstream commits a year) are the recurring cost.
3. The grafts contradict each other: schema_name vs Hospital.uuid prefixes, and expand/contract vs a 503 gate vs a maintenance window. CARE ships contract migrations (emr/0082).
4. Putting every isolation check, mutation run, restore drill and Playwright test on every push would multiply CI time several times over. Split them into tiers.
5. Deny-list blocking of auth endpoints, the twelve views that set their own authentication_classes, and fixtures-per-route crawls all fail open, or stall each sync. Use a fail-closed route allow-list and a generated crawl.
6. Settings-overlay drift can silently lose tenant isolation or make CI test non-tenant mode: TENANT_APPS lists, index-based middleware insertion, test.py redefining CACHES, upstream env setting DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE. Add a startup system check.
7. The tenant-mode CARE suite will fail on its thread-based tests unless the runner sets the schema on new connections.
8. Refdata packs are coupled to Spec churn; hash only pack-owned fields.
9. Plan the Keycloak refresh/logout through a backend shim rather than a large Login.tsx patch.
No simpler alternative reaches the same safety at the target density. Instance-per-tenant needs zero patches but costs too much RAM. Still, ADR-002's requirement to prototype both options must be met or explicitly amended.
